How I Approach Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome (MALS) and Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome (SMAS)
  • Source: American Journal of Gastroenterology, Vol. [Ahead of Print]
  • Topic: Underrecognized abdominal compression syndromes
  • Author(s): Zachary Spiritos, MD; Daniel Shouhed, MD; Alexis Cutchins, MD
Overview: Both Syndromes
  • MALS and SMAS are underrecognized abdominal compression syndromes
  • Present to GI clinics because symptoms resemble common motility diagnoses and disorders of brain-gut interaction (DBGI)
  • Often misdiagnosed as functional dyspepsia or irritable bowel syndrome
  • May be mistaken for eating disorders → biases clinicians against considering structural causes
  • Patients can go years without diagnosis
  • Undergo repeated testing and empiric trials of PPIs or neuromodulation without relief
  • Nutrition and quality of life decline over time
Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome (MALS)
Definition & Mechanism
  • Foregut compression disorder
  • Median arcuate ligament compresses the celiac artery and surrounding nerve plexus
  • Ligament = fibrous arch formed by convergence of right and left diaphragmatic crura
  • When ptotic (drooping) → compresses celiac artery and plexus
  • Often seen in connective tissue disorders (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)
  • Growing evidence supports a neurogenic mechanism as meaningful contributor
  • Mesenteric circulation provides substantial collateral flow → isolated ischemia unlikely
  • Relieving vascular compression alone often fails to provide durable relief
Clinical Presentation
  • Stereotypic presentation with epigastric pain shortly after eating/drinking (minutes)
  • Pain largely independent of meal or beverage size
  • Squeezing or pressure-like pain → like crushing sensation of a vice grip
  • Radiation: along left subcostal margin or to the back
  • Pain worsens with:
  • Physical activity
  • Deep exhalation → upward diaphragmatic movement increases tension on median arcuate ligament
  • Over time: postprandial pain → sitophobia (fear of eating) → weight loss
  • Often resembles functional dyspepsia early in disease course
Red Flags for MALS
  • Pain within minutes of eating or drinking
  • Lack of response to functional dyspepsia treatment
  • Weight loss
  • Comorbid connective tissue hypermobility
Diagnostic Evaluation
Step 1: Exclude Common Foregut Conditions
  • Rule out peptic ulcer disease and gastroparesis
  • Gastric emptying study can show delayed emptying (patients with hypermobility often have dysautonomia)
  • Delayed emptying may represent associated finding rather than primary driver
Step 2: Vascular Imaging (When Suspicion Remains High)
  • Obtain both:
  • Dynamic CT angiography
  • Mesenteric duplex ultrasound
CT Angiography Findings
  • Inspiratory and expiratory phases
  • Identifies signs of celiac artery compromise:
  • Focal narrowing with characteristic hooked configuration
  • Respiratory-dependent caliber changes
  • Post-stenotic dilatation
  • Note: Radiographic celiac artery compression can be seen in asymptomatic individuals
  • Imaging findings must always be interpreted in context of clinical presentation
Mesenteric Duplex Ultrasound
  • Evaluates hemodynamic relationship between median arcuate ligament and celiac artery
  • Expiratory peak systolic velocities:
  • >200 cm/s = abnormal → raises suspicion for compression
  • >350 cm/s = more specific for MALS
Step 3: Functional Testing (If Vascular Imaging Negative)
  • Celiac plexus block = primary diagnostic tool
  • Delivers local anesthetic + corticosteroid (more durable effect)
  • Therapeutic effect: transient (usually days to weeks)
  • Near-complete resolution of postprandial pain:
  • Supports diagnosis
  • Helps predict which patients will benefit from surgery
Management
Nutritional Stabilization
  • Patients frequently do not meet caloric needs at presentation
  • Post-pyloric enteral feeding via nasojejunal tube:
  • Provides nutritional rehabilitation during diagnostic process
  • Bypasses neural triggers → makes feeding less painful
  • Parenteral nutrition → reserved for patients who cannot tolerate enteral support
Definitive Treatment: Surgery
  • Surgical division of median arcuate ligament
  • Concurrent resection of celiac ganglion
  • Division of ligament alone → associated with high failure rates
  • Combined ganglionectomy results:
  • Improvement: roughly 85–90% of patients
  • Durable success at 5 years: approximately 65–70% (single-center series)
Postoperative Course
Most Common Complication
  • Transient diarrhea related to denervation of celiac plexus
Persistent Symptoms ≠ Surgical Failure
  • Patients often not free of digestive symptoms after neurectomy
  • Many have comorbid conditions:
  • Dysautonomia
  • Mast cell activation
  • Concomitant compression disorders:
  • SMAS
  • Pelvic venous disease
  • Longitudinal, multidisciplinary follow-up important for distinguishing:
  • Inadequate decompression
  • Associated pathology
Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome (SMAS)
Definition & Mechanism
  • Superior mesenteric artery and aorta compress the third portion of duodenum
  • Retroperitoneal fat pad normally maintains adequate separation
  • Conditions that reduce protective fat pad:
  • Narrow the aortomesenteric (AOM) angle
  • Precipitate syndrome
  • Causes:
  • Connective tissue laxity
  • Congenital predisposition
  • Acquired factors (most common: significant weight loss)
  • MALS is a frequent upstream contributor to SMAS
Clinical Presentation
  • Distinct picture from duodenal distention proximal to obstruction
  • Timing: 1–3 hours after eating (vs. MALS = minutes)
  • Symptoms:
  • Periumbilical pain
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Early satiety
  • Foods that provoke symptoms:
  • Bulky or high-residue foods
  • Raw vegetables
  • Fibrous fruits
  • Coarse grains
  • Tough meats
  • Food aversion → drives further weight loss → worsens compression
Diagnostic Evaluation
Step 1: Exclude Luminal Disease
  • Upper endoscopy:
  • Rules out mucosal pathology
  • Rules out gastric outlet obstruction
Step 2: Imaging Studies
  • CT with IV contrast + upper GI series with small bowel follow-through
  • CT permits measurement of AOM angle and distance:
  • Normal values:
  • Angle: 28–65 degrees
  • Distance: 10–28 mm
  • Suspicious for SMAS:
  • Angle <18 degrees
  • Distance <8 mm
Step 3: Functional Assessment
  • Upper GI series = functional study evaluating contrast passage through duodenum
  • Specific but not sensitive
  • Becomes abnormal only when compression causes contrast retention
Important Caveat
  • Narrowed AOM angle can be observed in asymptomatic individuals (especially thin people)
  • Radiographic measurements must be interpreted alongside compatible clinical presentation
Management
Conservative Measures
  • Therapeutic goal: Restore retroperitoneal fat pad via nutritional support
  • Nasojejunal feeding:
  • Bypasses extrinsic compression
  • Often necessary to meet caloric requirements
  • Parenteral nutrition → reserved for patients who cannot tolerate enteral feeds
Limitations of Conservative Treatment
  • Long-term compression → irreversible duodenal narrowing with impaired motility
  • Conservative measures lead to symptom resolution in only 10–30% of cases
When Surgery Required
  • Obstructive physiology persists despite conservative management
Surgical Options
Duodenojejunostomy
  • Most common surgical approach
  • Results are variable
Intestinal Derotation with Duodenoduodenostomy
  • Promising but still novel approach
  • Long-term follow-up data lacking
Postoperative Course
Challenging Recovery Factors
  • Underlying conditions complicate recovery:
  • Connective tissue disorders
  • Mast cell activation
  • Dysautonomia
Common Postoperative Issues
  • Many experience:
  • Persistent nausea
  • Abdominal pain
  • Delayed return of motility
  • Frequently require:
  • Temporary gastric decompression
  • Jejunal feeding
Recovery Timeline
  • Ranges from several weeks to several months
  • Realistic expectations should be discussed before surgery
Comparison: MALS vs. SMAS vs. Functional Dyspepsia
Key Differentiating Features
Feature MALS SMAS Functional Dyspepsia
Primary mechanism Compression of celiac plexus ± artery Duodenal compression between SMA and aorta Disorder of gut-brain interaction
Symptom onset after eating Minutes 1–3 hours Minutes to 1 hour
Pain location Epigastric Periumbilical Epigastric
Predominant symptom drivers Postprandial neural stimulation Duodenal distension proximal to obstruction Impaired gastric accommodation, visceral hypersensitivity, duodenal microinflammation
Food triggers Any solid/liquid Bulky or high-residue foods Large meals, spicy/high-fat foods
Weight loss Common Common Rare and usually mild
Effect of exertion/deep exhalation Often worsens symptoms No consistent effect No consistent effect
Associated conditions Hypermobility, dysautonomia Hypermobility, dysautonomia, rapid weight loss, scoliosis surgery Anxiety, depression
Clinical Pearls & Take-Home Points
Why These Syndromes Are Missed
  • Symptoms overlap with common motility disorders and DBGI
  • Often misdiagnosed as functional dyspepsia or IBS
Keys to Early Recognition
  • Careful attention to:
  • Symptom timing (minutes vs. hours)
  • Reproducibility
  • Weight loss
  • Comorbid hypermobility
Patient Selection for Surgery
  • Best outcomes with:
  • Compatible symptom pattern
  • Corroborating imaging findings
  • Excluding more common pathology
Multidisciplinary Care
  • Critical team includes:
  • Gastroenterology
  • Surgery
  • Nutrition
Prognosis
  • Both MALS and SMAS are treatable causes of severe GI morbidity
  • Early intervention can dramatically alter patient's clinical trajectory
